title: WELLS v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary: In Wells v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Jesse Wells, is a British national who, together with his wife and five children, identifies as a Gypsy—a group included within the Council of Europe’s definition of Roma and Travellers. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller families facing eviction from land they own due to planning regulations, and the difficulties in securing lawful accommodation that respects their traditional way of life. In April 2002, Mr. Wells moved his family and caravans onto Ashbrook Farm in Buckinghamshire, having previously lived on his father’s established Gypsy site. Shortly after, the local council served an enforcement notice requiring removal of the caravans, citing harm to the rural character of the area. Despite appeals and evidence of a shortage of Gypsy sites, the authorities maintained the enforcement, and Mr. Wells was ultimately convicted for non-compliance after a protracted legal process. He argued before the European Court of Human Rights that his rights under Articles 8 (private and family life), 14 (non-discrimination), and 6 (fair trial) of the Convention had been violated. However, the Court declared the application inadmissible, finding no appearance of a violation. This case highlights the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller families face in securing culturally appropriate accommodation in the UK, reflecting broader historical patterns of marginalisation and legal obstacles.
